topic: Lambda Capture Mode Lvalue Conversion via `std::bind`
explanation: Assumption: When simulating move capture using `std::bind` (e.g., passing `std::move(data)`), the stored object inside the bind object retains its rvalue properties or is treated as an rvalue upon invocation. Reality: Although the stored object may be initialized via move construction, the object itself, when accessed inside the bind object's invocation, is treated as an lvalue. Why It Fails: The parameter passed to the underlying callable (the lambda) corresponding to the stored object is an lvalue reference (or reference-to-const). This is critical for understanding how state is managed when using `std::bind` as a replacement for C++14 'init capture' or when passing resources to a deferred execution object.
code_example:
// data is moved into func, but accessed as an lvalue inside the lambda
auto func = std::bind([](Data& d) { /* d is an lvalue reference */ }, std::move(data));
practical_example: A developer uses `std::bind` to capture a unique pointer, expecting to call `std::move` on the parameter inside the lambda. Because the parameter is received as an lvalue reference (by default, a copy/reference of the stored object), the subsequent move operation might be overlooked or incorrectly implemented, leading to unintended copies or misuse of the moved-in resource.
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
